executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the contested status of women in American public life, spanning both elite sport and national politics. The Atlantic's longform analysis identifies masculinism as the organizing ideological force of the American right, built on the demonstrably false premise that feminism has damaged the country — a movement that seeks to roll back women's professional and political standing. That ideological backdrop makes The Athletic's reporting on the WNBA's officiating problem more than a sports story; it reflects a broader pattern in which women's professional achievement operates under scrutiny and institutional friction that male counterparts rarely face. Together, these two pieces reveal a cultural moment in which women's legitimacy — whether on a basketball court or in the workplace — is actively being challenged by coordinated forces, making the question of institutional fairness toward women one of the most consequential and underexamined stories of the day.

items.headline: Wemby's World: Did the Spurs star really just do that to OKC?
items.blurb: Forty-eight minutes and 42 seconds. Forty-one points. Twenty-four rebounds. Three assists. Three blocks. One massive 28-foot 3-pointer. That was Victor Wembanyama's stat line from the Spurs' 122-115 double-overtime victory in Game 1 of the Western Conference finals last night. Since blocked shots started being recorded in the 1973-74 season, only three players have put up 40 points, 24 boards and three blocks in a playoff game. Hakeem Olajuwon did it twice in 1987 and 1988. Shaquille O'Neal did it in 2000. Now Wemby.

newsletters.title: Here’s why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI

items.headline: Here's why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI
items.blurb:
Elon Musk has lost his lawsuit against OpenAI, which centered on whether the company breached its founding contract as a nonprofit. A jury found that he sued too late, meaning his claims are barred by statutes of limitations. But the verdict didn't judge if OpenAI violated its nonprofit mission—only whether Musk brought the case in time.

The dispute hinged on when OpenAI began shifting toward a for-profit structure. The company argued that signs of a shift were visible as early as 2017, while Musk said he only discovered the change in 2022.

items.headline: Inside Anduril and Meta's quest to make smart glasses for warfare
items.blurb:
The defense-tech company Anduril has shared new details about the augmented-reality headset for the military it's prototyping with Meta, including a vision for ordering drone strikes via eye-tracking and voice commands.

Quay Barnett, who leads the effort at Anduril following a career in the Army's Special Operations Command, says he aims to optimize "the human as a weapons system."

items.headline: What to expect at Google I/O this week
items.blurb:
When Google opens its doors today for its annual developer conference, I/O, it will do so as a clear third place in the foundation model race.

A foundation model's reputation these days rests largely on its coding capabilities, and for months Google's coding tools have been outgunned by Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex. But the company still shapes the cutting edge in areas such as AI for science. At I/O this week, it will try to prove it can compete on both fronts.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
As the limits of LLMs become clearer, researchers are developing a new kind of AI designed to understand the physical environment: world models.

Recent developments from Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Yann LeCun's new startup have pushed these systems to the forefront of AI. At an upcoming virtual event, MIT Technology Review will examine the progress—and what comes next.

items.headline: Just … how, Wemby?
items.blurb: Nothing said about Victor Wembanyama today will qualify as hyperbole. Wembanyama scored 41 points and grabbed 24 rebounds in the win, which gives the Spurs a 1-0 lead in the Western Conference finals over the defending champs.

Montreal took an early 2-0 lead in the first period, but that melted to a 2-2 tie in the third. The Canadiens advance to the Eastern Conference final for the first time since 2021 and get there via two consecutive Game 7 road wins.

items.headline: The PWHL handled business in regulation — barely
items.blurb: Like their city mates, the Montreal Victoire had a chance to close out a series last night, but this was for a title, and the Victoire were 5:30 away from a clean sweep of the Walter Cup Finals. As if they drew it up in a kid's backyard dream, the Ottawa Charge scored two goals in that final 5:30 to turn a 1-0 deficit into a 2-1 lead. Ottawa saved its season and prevented Montreal from celebrating on its ice. Game 4 is Wednesday in Ottawa.

longform.title: Why I don’t buy masculinism
longform.thesis: Masculinism—a coordinated ideological movement seeking to reverse women's political and professional gains—has become the dominant cohesive force on the American right, and its central claims that feminism has ruined America are unsupported by evidence.
longform.context: This is an author's note accompanying Helen Lewis's June 2026 Atlantic cover story, written as masculinist figures gain mainstream political proximity (e.g., Pete Hegseth) and high-profile thinkers openly advocate repealing the Nineteenth Amendment and restoring patriarchal economic structures.
arguments: Masculinism is not a fringe phenomenon but an organized movement with named ideologues—Douglas Wilson, Raw Egg Nationalist, Helen Andrews—whose demands include repealing women's suffrage, instituting a 'family wage,' and reversing the 'great feminization' of professional life, placing them in direct opposition to gains made since 1857.

The movement's ideological core targets empathy specifically, framing it as 'a dangerous, feminine softness toward immigrants and criminals,' which reveals masculinism's function as a broader right-wing binding agent rather than a narrow gender grievance.

Lewis distinguishes legitimate concern about male struggles—citing data that the majority of problem gamblers are male—from the masculinists' bad-faith claim that feminism is the cause of male decline, refusing to conflate the two and rejecting the 'Make Patriarchy Great Again' prescription.

Feminism's very success explains the intensity of the backlash: Lewis opens by arguing that movements 'inspire so much hate' precisely because they have been 'incredibly successful,' framing masculinism as a reactionary response to documented, extraordinary female advancement.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it names masculinism as 'the single most important force holding together the American right,' a analytical claim that reframes gender politics as a structural pillar of contemporary conservatism rather than a cultural sideshow. It also arrives at a moment when masculinist figures hold or influence federal power, making the ideology's policy implications immediate rather than theoretical. By refusing to dismiss all male grievance while rejecting masculinist diagnosis, Lewis attempts to hold analytical ground that mainstream discourse has largely ceded.
questions_raised: If some male struggles are real and underreported, what non-masculinist policy framework would Lewis endorse to address them—and does the cover story answer this, or leave it unresolved?

The piece asserts masculinism is 'the single most important force holding together the American right,' but does not—in this note—explain what displaces or subsumes other traditional right-wing unifiers like religion, nationalism, or economic conservatism, leaving the causal mechanism unexplored.
